screens.title: Player Settings: Identity and Build Defaults
screens.narratorSegment: The Player Settings panel is the single place where your game's identity and many platform defaults live. It includes fields such as Company Name, Product Name, and Version that determine how the operating system and stores reference your game. Company and Product strings often influence install folder names and store metadata, so consistency matters for updates and platform recognition. The Version field is central to release management: use a Major. Minor. Patch pattern so you and your distribution channels can understand the scope of a change. A concrete example: if you publish version 1.0.0 and then add a small bug fix, increment to 1.0.1. If you add a new feature that doesn't break compatibility, increase the Minor number, for example to 1.1.0. A common misconception is treating version as decorative text; instead, treat it as a formal release identifier used by patching systems and stores. In Player Settings you will also find platform-specific fields for bundle identifiers and scripting backends—these can affect compatibility and build behavior. The key takeaway is to complete identity fields early and maintain them consistently as part of your release checklist.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Player Settings
Core Concept

Player Settings: Identity

Fields here affect how the OS and stores refer to your game and where build files are placed on a device.

Identification Fields
  • Company Name: Defines company-level folder and store metadata.
  • Product Name: The game title shown in OS and file locations.
  • Version: Use Major.Minor.Patch to track releases.
Example
If your current build is 1.0.0 and you fix a crash, update to 1.0.1. For a new gameplay feature without breaking saves, update to 1.1.0.
Common Mistake

Leaving version blank or inconsistent across builds causes confusion when submitting updates and can trigger store rejections or user confusion during patching.

Quick Checklist
  • Set Company and Product early.
  • Adopt Major.Minor.Patch and document increments.
  • Confirm bundle IDs and scripting backend for each platform.
Key Takeaway

Identity fields are functional: fill them consistently to ensure proper installs and store listings.

screens.title: Versioning Strategy: Major.Minor.Patch
screens.narratorSegment: A clear versioning strategy prevents confusion for players and distribution platforms. The widely used Major. Minor. Patch pattern signals the scope of changes. Major increments indicate significant updates or breaking changes, Minor increments add features or improvements that preserve compatibility, and Patch increments fix bugs or small issues. A practical workflow: before every build you plan to release, update the Version field in Player Settings and record the change in your release notes. For example, move from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 for a performance fix, or to 1.1.0 when adding a new level. This consistency matters when platforms compare versions for updates or when players expect backward compatibility. A common misconception is overloading the Major number for marketing; keep Major changes reserved for large shifts because many platform tools and scripts use versioning to decide upgrade paths. Use your version number in packaging names and store submissions so every build is traceable. The takeaway: adopt the pattern early and make version updates part of the build checklist to avoid accidental overwrites or mismatched store submissions. Versioning Strategy: Major.Minor.Patch means update the version field before each release and reflect that number in your build artifacts and release notes.. In practical terms, a repeatable scheme to communicate changes and manage updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Versioning Strategy
Process Flow
Major.Minor.Patch
  1. Major: Breaking changes, large feature sets or engine upgrades.
  2. Minor: New features that remain backwards compatible.
  3. Patch: Bug fixes, small tweaks, or performance improvements.
Concrete Example
Imagine releasing 1.0.0. You patch a crash found in the physics system and publish 1.0.1. Later you add a new multiplayer lobby system without breaking saved games and publish 1.1.0. If you later overhaul save compatibility, you move to 2.0.0.
Common Misconception

Some teams use dates or marketing labels instead of semantic versioning; that complicates automated tooling and patch identification. Semantic versioning keeps machine and human expectations aligned.

Key Takeaway

Adopt Major.Minor.Patch early and include version bumps in your release checklist and artifact names.

screens.title: Icons and Splash Image
screens.narratorSegment: Icons and splash images are small but powerful branding signals. The game icon is visible on desktops, mobile home screens, and store listings; it must be recognizable at small sizes and comply with platform-specific size and format requirements. Unity lets you assign different icons for different resolutions and platforms so your icon retains clarity whether shown at 48 pixels or 1024 pixels. The splash image appears during loading and is often the first thing a player sees. Even with Unity's free version, you can place a custom image that appears before the Unity logo; this is a key branding opportunity. Optimize splash art for both visual clarity and file size — large uncompressed images can add unnecessary loading time. A concrete example: provide a 512x512 square icon for use as a default and then supply higher-resolution replacements for stores and high-DPI devices. A frequent mistake is dragging a large PSD and not exporting flattened, compressed PNGs for each required size. The takeaway: prepare a small set of exported, platform-sized assets and assign them in Player Settings so the game looks professional across devices.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Icons & Splash
Definition

Icons

Supply platform-sized icons. Unity supports per-platform icon assignments so they remain crisp at every display size.

Best Practices
  • Export flattened PNGs at required sizes.
  • Test icon readability at small sizes.
  • Provide high-DPI variants for app stores and desktops.

Splash Image

Use a simple branded image and optimize for load size. Even if Unity's logo appears later, a custom image ahead of it improves brand recall.

Concrete Example

Add a 1024x512 compressed PNG for landscape splash and a square 512x512 for icon use, then assign them in the Splash Image and Icon sections.

Key Takeaway

Prepare and optimize a small set of exported assets to assign per platform for fast, clear branding.

screens.title: Resolution & Presentation: Desktop vs Mobile
screens.narratorSegment: Resolution and presentation settings control how your game window behaves and how the UI scales on different devices. On desktop builds you typically choose whether to launch fullscreen, windowed, or allow the player to decide. You can also set default resolutions and preferred aspect ratios. On mobile, presentation often centers on orientation—portrait or landscape—and how the game scales to varied screen sizes. The practical difference is that desktop users often expect freedom to change window size, while mobile users expect a responsive layout that adapts to many physical resolutions. A concrete example: set desktop default to 1920x1080 fullscreen, but for mobile, enforce landscape orientation and use Unity's Canvas Scaler to keep HUD elements anchored and proportional. A common pitfall is not testing UI across aspect ratios; text or buttons can be cut off on narrow phones or ultra-wide monitors. The best practice is to design responsive UI with safe zones and anchors, and to test builds on representative devices or simulation modes. The core insight: presentation defaults shape the player's experience and must align with your primary platform expectations. Resolution & Presentation: Desktop vs Mobile means choose presentation defaults that match player expectations per platform and test ui responsiveness across aspect ratios.. In practical terms, how defaults and scaling differ between target device classes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Resolution & Presentation
Comparison

Desktop

  • Windowed vs fullscreen defaults.
  • Set default resolution and allow user resizing.
  • Test UI across widescreen monitors.
Mobile
  • Default orientation (portrait or landscape).
  • Scaling rules and Canvas Scaler settings.
  • Test on multiple aspect ratios and DPI ranges.
Concrete Scenario

If your game targets phones and tablets, choose an orientation and design UI with anchors and safe margins. Use a Canvas Scaler in scale-with-screen-size mode and test a 16:9 phone and a 4:3 tablet to find layout issues.

Common Mistake

Assuming pixel-perfect layouts will translate across devices. Instead, rely on responsive anchors and proportional scaling so elements remain visible and usable.

Key Takeaway

Match presentation defaults to the typical user environment and validate UI across representative resolutions.

screens.title: Canvas Scaler & UI Responsiveness
screens.narratorSegment: Responsive UI is essential for a polished release. Unity's Canvas Scaler component controls how UI elements scale with screen size. The common mode is 'Scale With Screen Size' where you set a reference resolution and a match mode that weights width versus height. Combined with anchors and pivot points on RectTransforms, this keeps buttons and HUD elements in predictable locations across screens. A concrete example: set a reference resolution of 1920x1080 and anchor the health bar to the top-left with safe offsets; on narrow phones it will keep its relative position without being cut off. A common misconception is that fixed pixel positions are sufficient; they are not. Without anchors and a scaler, UI will drift or clip at different aspect ratios. Also test text scaling and consider minimum sizes to maintain readability. The practical workflow before release: build for a small selection of device form factors, inspect critical screens, and iterate on anchors and scaler match until UI remains usable. The takeaway is to treat UI scaling as an early release checkpoint rather than a last-minute fix. Canvas Scaler & UI Responsiveness means use canvas scaler + anchors; test on multiple aspect ratios to ensure ui elements remain visible and readable.. In practical terms, how to design ui that adapts to different screens and aspect ratios. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Canvas Scaler & UI
Definition

Canvas Scaler

Set a reference resolution and choose a match between width and height so UI scales predictably.

Practical Steps
  1. Attach Canvas Scaler and set reference resolution (e.g., 1920x1080).
  2. Choose Scale With Screen Size and set match mode to suit your UI layout.
  3. Anchor HUD elements to corners and set safe offsets.
  4. Test on representative device resolutions.
Example

Anchor a top-right score counter to the top-right corner and set scale to match height slightly more if your UI stacks vertically on phones.

Misconception

Relying on fixed pixel layouts may look fine in the editor but fails on different aspect ratios. Use scalable layout components instead.

Key Takeaway

Design UI to scale; test early and often on multiple aspect ratios to avoid last-minute fixes.

screens.title: Quality Settings Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Quality Settings in Unity provide a matrix of preset levels—'Fastest,' 'Good,' 'Fantastic,' and more—that control rendering parameters such as texture resolution, anti-aliasing, shadow quality, and VSync. Each preset is a bundle of settings you can customize and assign as defaults per platform. The practical use is to pick an appropriate default for each target: mobile devices usually default to lower presets to preserve frame rate, while PC builds can use higher presets for richer visuals. For example, toggling anti-aliasing from off to 4x MSAA increases visual smoothness but also G P U cost. A common misconception is to enable the highest presets by default; instead, choose defaults that match the lowest acceptable hardware you intend to support and expose in-game graphics options for players to raise fidelity. The best workflow is to profile performance at multiple quality levels on representative hardware and choose the preset that hits your target frame rate with acceptable visual quality. This chapter prepares you to customize presets and to assign platform defaults so the first shipped build behaves as expected on each device class. Quality Settings Overview means use quality presets to define consistent rendering behavior per platform and test them on representative hardware.. In practical terms, preset levels that balance visual fidelity against performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Quality Settings
Core Concept

Quality Presets

Each preset groups render settings like texture size, shadows, and anti-aliasing. Customize them to fit hardware targets.

Fast
Low textures, no AA, minimal shadows.
Good
Balanced settings for mid-range hardware.
Fantastic
High textures, 4x AA, soft shadows, reflections enabled.
Testing Advice

Profile your game on representative devices at each preset. Aim for the target frame rate at the default preset for each platform.

Misconception

Higher defaults improve visuals but may frustrate players on low-end hardware. Provide options and sensible defaults instead.

Key Takeaway

Define and test presets; assign platform defaults that hit your performance goals while preserving acceptable visuals.

screens.title: Customizing a Quality Level
screens.narratorSegment: Customizing quality levels lets you tune the visual/performance trade-off for your project. Start by selecting an existing preset such as 'Fantastic' and make incremental changes: for example, set anti-aliasing to 4x multi-sampling to smooth edges and change shadow quality to 'Hard and Soft' to support mixed shadow modes. Every change affects G P U cost and memory; adjust one parameter at a time and measure the impact using the Unity Profiler or platform-specific tools. A concrete workflow: duplicate the 'Fantastic' preset, rename it to 'Fantastic-MobileTuned', reduce texture size or anisotropic filtering, then reduce shadow distance and disable real-time reflections. Assign this custom preset as the default for your target mobile platform in the Quality Settings matrix. A common misconception is that toggling a single setting like anti-aliasing will not substantially change performance; in reality, some settings have outsized costs on certain devices. Always profile on representative hardware and iterate until the preset meets your frame rate and visual quality targets. This approach ensures polished visuals without compromising playability. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Customize Quality
Process Flow

Step-by-step

  1. Duplicate an existing preset and rename it for your target platform.
  2. Adjust one parameter, such as anti-aliasing or shadow distance.
  3. Build and profile on a representative device.
  4. Iterate until performance and visuals reach the target balance.
Concrete Change

Switch Anti Aliasing to 4x and set Shadows to Hard and Soft to improve perceived quality, then measure FPS change to see the cost.

Profiling Tip

Use the Unity Profiler and test scenes that stress rendering—shadows, reflections, and post-processing—to see real-world impacts.

Misconception

Assuming identical costs across devices is risky; some GPUs handle AA cheaply while others do not. Always test where your players will run the game.

Key Takeaway

Tune presets iteratively and assign custom levels as defaults for each platform to match hardware capabilities.

screens.title: Assigning Platform Defaults
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Quality Settings window provides a matrix that lets you select which quality preset should be the default for each target platform. This is a simple but powerful step: when you assign a default quality for Android, for example, builds for that platform inherit the chosen preset automatically. A practical workflow: create or tune presets first, then open the Quality Settings matrix and select the desired default column for each platform. For instance, choose 'Good' for standalone and a tuned 'Fast' for low-end Android devices. After assigning defaults, build each platform and test the resulting executable or package to verify the preset is applied. A common mistake is customizing a preset but forgetting to assign it as the platform default, resulting in unexpected visuals after building. Remember to document which preset you assign per platform so team members and automation scripts use the correct targets. The core idea is that platform defaults keep your shipped build predictable without requiring manual changes after the build step. Quality Matrix

Open Edit > Project Settings > Quality. Use the top row of the matrix to select each platform's default preset.

Concrete Example

After tuning 'Fast-Mobile' to reduce shadows and AA, set that preset as the default in the Android column so Android builds run with the tuned settings automatically.

Common Mistake

Forgetting to set platform defaults, or assuming editor playback uses the same preset as the build. Always test the built application on device.

Key Takeaway

Assign and verify platform defaults so builds run with intended quality settings without manual steps after building.

Quick Checklist

You are at the final polish stage: the place where a prototype becomes a product. In this lesson you will learn which Unity Editor settings determine how your game is identified, how it appears to players, and how it performs across devices. We will focus on the Player Settings panel for identity, icons, splash screens, resolution and presentation, and the Quality Settings panel for balancing visuals and performance. You will also learn a consistent versioning approach that helps track releases and communicate changes. For example, setting Company Name and Product Name correctly prevents confusing folder structures and store metadata issues. Choosing sensible default quality presets per platform avoids low frame rates on older hardware or unnecessarily low fidelity on capable devices. Throughout, we will highlight common mistakes—like inconsistent version numbers or neglecting UI testing across aspect ratios—and give practical steps to prevent them. By the end you will be able to configure the essential fields and create a repeatable release checklist that protects your first impression with players.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and configure the Player Settings fields that define your game's identity, set a systematic version number, and add platform-appropriate icons and a branded splash image. You will also understand how resolution and presentation choices affect desktop and mobile behavior, and how the Canvas Scaler and anchors protect UI layout across devices. Finally, you will learn how Unity's Quality Settings provide preset levels that control texture resolutions, anti-aliasing, and shadow detail, and how to assign sensible default presets per platform. For example, when targeting mobile you will select a lower default quality to preserve frame rate; for PC you might choose higher defaults. This chapter includes a hands-on task that walks through setting Company Name, Product Name, Version, and adding icon and splash assets. It also teaches a practical versioning rule—Major. Minor. Patch—so you can communicate release scope to players and stores. These objectives help ensure your game installs correctly, looks professional, and runs acceptably on your intended devices.

This continuation outlines the practical skills you will practice so they become routine. You will learn to assign default quality levels per platform and to customize a quality level by changing parameters like anti-aliasing and shadow mode. You will practice adding icons sized for different platform requirements and composing a splash image optimized for loading time. The lesson also covers resolution and presentation choices, including windowed versus fullscreen defaults for desktop and orientation and scaling rules for mobile. For each setting, we discuss testing strategies: run builds on representative hardware and use the Canvas Scaler to keep UI elements anchored. A common misconception is that higher visual settings always equal better user experience; instead, the right default is what provides a consistent frame rate for your target audience. By practicing these skills you will build a release checklist that saves time and avoids store rejections or poor first impressions.

The Player Settings panel is the single place where your game's identity and many platform defaults live. It includes fields such as Company Name, Product Name, and Version that determine how the operating system and stores reference your game. Company and Product strings often influence install folder names and store metadata, so consistency matters for updates and platform recognition. The Version field is central to release management: use a Major. Minor. Patch pattern so you and your distribution channels can understand the scope of a change. A concrete example: if you publish version 1.0.0 and then add a small bug fix, increment to 1.0.1. The key takeaway is to complete identity fields early and maintain them consistently as part of your release checklist.

A clear versioning strategy prevents confusion for players and distribution platforms. The widely used Major. Minor. Patch pattern signals the scope of changes. Icons and splash images are small but powerful branding signals. The game icon is visible on desktops, mobile home screens, and store listings; it must be recognizable at small sizes and comply with platform-specific size and format requirements. Unity lets you assign different icons for different resolutions and platforms so your icon retains clarity whether shown at 48 pixels or 1024 pixels. The splash image appears during loading and is often the first thing a player sees. Even with Unity's free version, you can place a custom image that appears before the Unity logo; this is a key branding opportunity. Resolution and presentation settings control how your game window behaves and how the UI scales on different devices. On desktop builds you typically choose whether to launch fullscreen, windowed, or allow the player to decide. You can also set default resolutions and preferred aspect ratios.
